query: Prior studies of Al-containing Cr–Co–Fe–Ni alloys showed that composition and thermal history can substantially alter constituent phases and transformation behavior, but they did not establish a predictive explanation of phase stability across the relevant thermal regime or adequately connect it to composition-dependent thermodynamic instability. Given the competing thermodynamic and kinetic factors in multicomponent alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state and why? State a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations, boundary conditions, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7, the stability of the high‐temperature BCC phase is governed by the thermodynamic driving force given by the CALPHAD‐derived difference in Gibbs free energies (ΔG_bcc–fcc) which, when combined with the kinetics of cooling, determines the degree of transformation to the fcc phase.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy in an initially high-temperature BCC state.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled cooling protocols from the high-temperature state, using a range from rapid quenching to slow cooling, while comparing the outcomes with CALPHAD-predicted ΔG_bcc–fcc values.
generation.conditions: All samples must have identical composition and be processed under an inert or controlled atmosphere to minimize extrinsic effects; the only variable is the controlled cooling rate to modulate available diffusion time.
generation.structural_mediator: The phase fractions of BCC and fcc (and possibly any intermediate structures) that emerge as a function of cooling rate.
generation.mechanism: The difference in Gibbs free energy (ΔG_bcc–fcc) drives the transformation from metastable BCC to the lower-energy fcc phase; however, the extent of the transformation is modulated by kinetic factors (cooling rate). Slow cooling provides sufficient time for atoms to rearrange into the equilibrium fcc structure, whereas rapid cooling kinetically arrests the system in the BCC state.
generation.predicted_outcome: Experiments with slower cooling rates will show an increased fraction of the fcc phase compared to samples subjected to rapid quenching. The observed phase distribution should correlate qualitatively with the computed ΔG_bcc–fcc values.
generation.baseline: A standard intermediate cooling rate experiment that produces a reproducible, mixed phase microstructure against which the effects of faster and slower cooling can be compared.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies within a cooling rate window where kinetic transformation can be effectively modulated. In the extreme limits—very slow cooling (allowing complete equilibrium) or very rapid quenching (completely suppressing short-range atomic diffusion)—the relationship between ΔG_bcc–fcc and phase stability may not be evident.
generation.uncertainty: The precise critical cooling rate at which the transformation becomes appreciable and the quantitative relationship between ΔG_bcc–fcc and phase fraction remain to be fully determined, as they may be influenced by subtle microstructural factors and experimental conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples in the high-temperature BCC state and subject them to a range of controlled cooling rates (e.g., rapid quench, intermediate cooling, and slow cooling). Use quantitative phase analysis techniques (such as X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy) to measure the fraction of fcc and BCC phases in each sample.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experiments show that slowing the cooling rate does not lead to a systematic and correlatable increase in the fcc phase fraction consistent with the CALPHAD-predicted ΔG_bcc–fcc values, then the hypothesis that the thermodynamic driving force (modulated by cooling kinetics) governs phase stability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Our results indicated that kinetics of phase transformation plays a crucial role in phase selection of the CoCrFeNiTi0.4 HEA. The phases can be controlled using kinetic ways according to the CCT curve. It seems that the sluggish diffusion in HEAs did not affect the kinetic behavior in this alloy system especially in the intermediate temperature. In fact, kinetic effect not only works for the special CoCrFeNiTi0.4 HEA but affects the phase selection of all HEAs. Li et al. reported that BCC phase can be obtained by supercooling method in the well-known FCC single phase CoCrFeNi HEA and the mechanical properties of the HEA was enhanced by three times. The rapid solidification behavior of CoCrCuNiFex HEA was also studied and useful nano-phases were found in the matrix, which would unquestionably strengthen the HEA dramatically. Ravi et al. reported that synthesis route can have a significant influence on the process of phase-choice and -evolution in different HEAs and this is actually a result of kinetic effect. cited_evidence.kind: web:Alloy design based on CALPHAD approach
cited_evidence.text: To generate the fcc to bcc martensitic transformation, we adopt the following strategies: (1) to obtain a single fcc phase in the as-annealed state and (2) to increase the thermal stability of bcc phase at low temperature. It is well known that a key parameter for designing metastable MEAs as well as conventional structural alloys which show the TRIP behavior, i.e., the fcc to bcc transformation, is the stacking fault energy (SFE) of fcc. Though the SFE contains a term expressed by a difference in Gibbs free energies between hcp and fcc phases,,, the fcc to bcc transformation is also analyzed by the SFE. In this study, however, we reveal that a difference in Gibbs free energies between bcc and fcc phases can be a critical parameter for the fcc to bcc martensitic transformation. The phase equilibrium and stability were calculated by using a Thermo-Calc software along with the thermodynamic database TCFE2000 and its upgraded version. This CALPHAD approach is much more effective than trial-and-error-based conventional alloy-design approaches consuming a lot of costs and time,. The above results reveal that our design approach based on the difference in Gibbs free energies between bcc and fcc phases (ΔGbcc-fcc) can realize the fcc to bcc transformation in MEA research areas. The fraction of bcc and consequent transformation rate according to the Co content and temperature also well correspond to the thermodynamic phase stability. In this section, we discuss the microstructural evolution and phase stability, varied with the balance of Co and Ni, and their contributions to the mechanical response in detail.

reading.lever: Combine CALPHAD‐derived ΔG_bcc–fcc predictions with controlled kinetic (cooling rate) measurements in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
reading.why: Because this integrated simulation and kinetic approach directly links composition-dependent thermodynamic instability with phase transformation behavior, addressing the limitation of prior studies.
